These are not wings. They are living membranes stretched over flexible ribs. Within them, colonies of microscopic organisms absorb the dim sunlight and supply the grazer with sugars. Tiny channels carry nutrient-rich fluid through the sails, forming patterns like frost on a window. A healthy animal’s sails shimmer copper and rose; a starving one’s become almost clear.

During violent weather, the sails fold into grooves along its spine. A sudden gust can make an entire herd collapse its bright crests at once, as though someone has extinguished a field of lanterns.

The grazer’s head hangs beneath the front of its body on a short, muscular neck. Instead of jaws, it has a circular feeding pad fringed with hundreds of soft, fingerlike projections. It presses this pad against the marsh floor, loosens mineral crusts with a sour secretion, and draws up the mats of microbes growing underneath. In the quiet, its feeding makes a sound like someone slowly peeling damp cloth from stone.

It has no eyes.

An old grazer is unmistakable. Its sails are patched and cloudy, its armor furred with tiny violet growths. When it finally dies, the sails sag into the marsh, where their microbial inhabitants continue growing in the shallow water.
